summary:
Outpost Shift is a pixel-art game for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in any web browser. You pick an astronaut, get briefed by Dr. Vega, and then look after a Moon outpost for 20 days. Every day you share 8 units of power between life support, the radiation shield and science, go outside to do research, and sleep to end the day. If the air runs out or the radiation gets too high, the crew is lost. If you make it through, you go home and get a mission report graded D to S.

It addresses the challenge of training junior astronauts by letting kids practice the job. The storms come from real NASA DONKI space-weather data: solar flares, particle events and coronal mass ejections. Echo, the ship’s AI, gives a daily forecast that can be wrong, so players learn to plan when they aren’t sure.

It matters because space weather is real but hard for children to picture. In the game they feel why it matters through their own choices. Art was made with Google Gemini, and code and sounds with Anthropic Claude. All of it is disclosed. The game is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
What it does: Outpost Shift is a browser game for ages 7 to 12. You run a Moon outpost for 20 days. Each day you share 8 units of power between life support, the radiation shield and science, then do research outside and sleep. If the air runs out or radiation gets too high, the crew is lost. If you survive, you go home and get a mission report graded D to S.

NASA data: The storms come from NASA’s DONKI database: solar flares, particle events and coronal mass ejections. The game plays the busiest 20 of the last 30 days. Echo, the ship’s AI, gives a forecast that can be wrong. If NASA can’t be reached, a labelled practice schedule is used.

Impact: Space weather is real but hard to picture. The game lets kids feel it through their own choices. We haven’t tested whether it teaches this, so it is our goal, not a result.

Tools: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Web Audio API for sounds, and the NASA DONKI API. The art was made with Google Gemini. The code and sounds were assisted by Anthropic Claude. All AI use is disclosed.

Creative: a retro pixel style, a story with characters, and a sky and storms that follow real data.

We considered: simple wording for kids, honest forecasts, balanced difficulty, keyboard and touch controls, and a mute button. The radiation limit and grading are game rules we chose, not NASA figures.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI: Solar Energetic Particle events (SEP)
